passage: Gargi had moved to Mumbai in January, and in the third week of March everything went wrong at once. On Monday her pitch was rejected in front of the whole client team. On Tuesday the fever started. By Wednesday night she lay in her rented room in Andheri, sheets damp, kettle empty, rain hammering on the tin sunshade. No Maa bringing rasam, no cousin two streets away. She scrolled flights home and whispered, 'What was I thinking, coming here?' Her thumb hovered over Neelam's name, the quiet designer from the next desk; they had shared lunch exactly twice. She typed, 'Sorry, bit random, I'm unwell and alone, is there a chemist that delivers?' Neelam called within minutes and arrived an hour later with soup, a thermometer and the number of a nearby clinic. 'If it doesn't settle, we'll go together,' Neelam said. Gargi cried from relief.

qa.q: What did Neelam bring?
qa.a: Soup, a thermometer and the number of a nearby clinic.

qa.q: What does Gargi scrolling flights home suggest about her state of mind?
qa.a: Her doubt about the move had peaked; ill and alone after a setback, she questioned why she had come at all.

qa.q: What turned the stretch for Gargi?
qa.a: Reaching out to Neelam, though they barely knew each other, brought care and a plan to see a doctor together if the fever did not settle.

qa.q: What might it be like for Neelam to get Gargi's message?
qa.a: Neelam may be surprised but moved to be trusted, and responds quickly, perhaps knowing how alone a new city can feel.

grounding: Shows a low point after a work setback and illness in a new city, where doubt peaks and reaching out to a colleague turns things.

passage:
'Chandu akka, don't panic, okay?' Sachin said, his face grey on the video call.
'Now I'm panicking. What happened?'
'The project I've been on since I moved here got scrapped. Four months, gone. And the landlord says the flat's being sold.'
'Oh, Sachin.'
'I don't know anyone here to even rant to. I walked around Hitech City for two hours so I wasn't just sitting in the room.'
'Have you eaten?'
'Chips.'
'Sachin.'
He laughed weakly. 'I keep thinking I should just come back to Vizag. Maybe this was a mistake.'
'Maybe. Maybe not. Don't decide in your worst week.' Chandrika pulled her laptop closer. 'Tonight, order real food. Tomorrow, call that college senior you mentioned, Ravi. And call me every evening this week, even for two minutes.'
'Every evening?'
'Every evening. I'm your net until you build one here.'

qa.q: How long did Sachin walk around Hitech City?
qa.a: For two hours.

qa.q: What is Sachin worried he got wrong at this point?
qa.a: He doubts the move itself, wondering if coming was a mistake after losing his project and his flat in the same week.

qa.q: What does Chandrika's advice get right?
qa.a: She tells him not to decide in his worst week and gives small steps: real food, a call to Ravi and a daily check-in with her.

qa.q: What is it like for Chandrika to see her brother this low?
qa.a: She is worried and briefly panicked, yet steadies herself to be his support until he builds his own 🫂

grounding: Illustrates the low point of a move, when a work setback and housing trouble without local support make doubt peak, and reaching out helps.

passage:
Monday: Maria's fever started at the office. By evening in her new Hyderabad flat, she was shivering under two blankets with nobody to ask for water. She went to the clinic nearby and came back with medicine and a strange loneliness.

Wednesday: Still weak, she opened her laptop and found an email: the client had rejected her whole proposal. She sat on the kitchen floor and thought, why did I leave Goa? Everyone I know is there. She typed a resignation note and saved it.

Friday: Almost without deciding to, she messaged Disha, a teammate she'd had lunch with twice: "Sorry to bother you. I'm sick and it's been a bad week." Twenty minutes later Disha replied: "Coming with khichdi. Address?"

That evening they sat on the floor and ate. Maria laughed for the first time all week, and deleted the resignation draft.

qa.q: What did Disha bring?
qa.a: Disha came with khichdi.

qa.q: What was Maria feeling on the kitchen floor on Wednesday?
qa.a: She felt defeated and full of doubt about the move, sick and alone, and even typed a resignation note.

qa.q: What turning point is available at this stage, and how did Maria use it?
qa.a: Reaching out to someone nearby; Maria's message to Disha brought company and food, which made the week feel survivable.

qa.q: What is it like for Disha to get Maria's message?
qa.a: Disha likely felt concerned and glad to be asked, responding quickly and warmly to a newer teammate.

grounding: Across one bad week, illness and a work setback in a new city feel much worse alone until reaching out to someone turns it.

passage:
Vandana, sit. You asked if I ever regretted leaving Bhopal. Let your Pranav mama tell you about one week.

I was twenty-four, new in Kolkata, a junior at a shipping firm. In my third month, it rained for four days straight. My room flooded, my shoes rotted, and I got a fever. Then my manager told me I'd made a mistake in a report, in front of everyone.

That Friday I sat on my bed with my feet in water and thought, I'll take the Sunday train home and never come back.

Instead, for no reason, I called Subrata, a quiet clerk from my office. I said, "My room is flooded." He came in an hour with a bucket and a flask of tea.

We're still friends. That call was the whole turning point, beta. Not the job, not the city. One phone call.

qa.q: What did Subrata bring when he came?
qa.a: He came with a bucket and a flask of tea.

qa.q: What was Pranav feeling that Friday on the bed with his feet in water?
qa.a: He felt defeated and alone, doubting the move so much that he planned to go home for good.

qa.q: What was the choice inside the story that changed things?
qa.a: Calling Subrata, a quiet colleague, and admitting he was struggling; that one call brought help and a lasting friendship.

qa.q: How might Subrata have felt when Pranav called?
qa.a: Subrata may have been surprised but glad to be trusted, and he felt enough care to come at once with help.

grounding: An elder recalls a low week in a new city, where illness and a work setback deepened doubt until reaching out turned it.

passage:
Madhuri's laptop was stolen from the Guwahati bus on Tuesday, two days before her project deadline, and the new city felt suddenly hostile.

She filed a report at the police station, then sat in a café with a cold coffee and no backup of her last week's work. She had no family here. Her friends were in Nagpur. The office knew her as the quiet new analyst.

The doubt came hard: What am I even doing here?

Her phone showed one name from the office she'd chatted with: Naveen, who had helped her find the canteen on day one. She almost didn't. Then she typed: "My laptop got stolen and I'm a bit lost. Do you know how IT handles this?"

He called back within minutes, walked her through the IT steps, and said, "Come in early tomorrow. We'll rebuild the slides together."

She paid for the coffee and, for the first time that day, breathed out.

qa.q: Where was Madhuri's laptop stolen?
qa.a: It was stolen from the Guwahati bus.

qa.q: What was Madhuri feeling in the café?
qa.a: She felt alone and overwhelmed, doubting her move to the city with no support nearby and a deadline looming.

qa.q: Which choice turned Madhuri's day, and why?
qa.a: Messaging Naveen despite barely knowing him; asking for help brought practical support and a small sense of belonging.

qa.q: How might Naveen see Madhuri's message?
qa.a: Naveen seems to see a new colleague in real trouble and wants to help, glad she thought of him.

grounding: With a stolen laptop and a deadline in an unfamiliar city, doubt peaks until reaching out to a colleague changes the stretch.

passage: In the second month of her job in Hyderabad, Trisha caught a fever the same week her first big presentation was torn apart by the client. She lay in her rented flat in Madhapur, sweating under two blankets, too weak to cook. There was no one to bring her rasam. Her phone showed messages from the office group about the presentation's "learnings." She thought, maybe I should just go back to Nagpur. Maybe this whole move was a mistake. At midnight, she scrolled to Maria, a colleague who had once shared lunch with her. She typed, "Sorry to bother, I'm unwell. Do you know a clinic nearby?" and almost deleted it. She sent it. Maria replied in five minutes: "Not a bother! There's one on my street. I'll take you tomorrow morning, and I'm bringing soup." Trisha put the phone on her chest and cried with relief.

qa.q: How quickly did Maria reply?
qa.a: Maria replied in five minutes.

qa.q: What was Trisha feeling before she sent the message to Maria?
qa.a: Trisha felt low and doubtful, sick and alone, wondering whether the whole move to Hyderabad had been a mistake.

qa.q: Why did the midnight message matter so much?
qa.a: Reaching out, even hesitantly, connected Trisha to someone who could help, which turned a very low week and gave her some support in the new city.

qa.q: How might Maria feel getting Trisha's message at midnight?
qa.a: Maria may feel concerned but glad to be asked, seeing it as a chance to help a new colleague who has no one nearby.

grounding: Shows a bad week of illness and a work setback in an unfamiliar city, doubt about the move peaking, and reaching out to someone turning the stretch.
